 Warning for New Jersey Senior Homeowners: Nov. 2 Deadline Puts Up to $6,500 at Risk
 Colleen Petrucci 
 10/27/2026 
 Photo: NJ Spotlight News (all rights reserved) 
 New Jersey residents have until Nov. 2 to apply for state property tax relief. Senior homeowners have the most at stake, with up to $6,500 in annual benefits, NJ Spotlight News reported. The deadline covers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ.
 Gov. Mikie Sherrill and lawmakers budgeted more than $4 billion this year for housing affordability benefits, including income tax deductions and direct rebates. ANCHOR, the state's most popular rebate, is funded with more than $2 billion.
 Property tax bills averaged a record $10,570 last year.
 Nov. 2, 2026 is the filing deadline for the 2025 application, according to the Division of Taxation's property tax relief page . "We want to ensure that all eligible residents take advantage of these programs designed to make New Jersey a more affordable place to live," State Treasurer Aaron Binder said in a news release, according to NJ Spotlight News .
 Who has to file
 The Division of Taxation filed ANCHOR applications automatically for most eligible homeowners under 65 and most renters of any age. It mailed benefit confirmation letters on Aug. 10. No letter? File on your own by Nov. 2.
 Seniors and people collecting Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability benefits must file the PAS-1, which checks eligibility for all three programs.
 Every homeowner 65 and older must file it even if they filed last year, said Marita Sciarrotta, director of the Division of Taxation, NJ101.5 reported. Treasury officials are urging residents who have not applied to do so before the deadline, NorthJersey.com reported.
 Other residents can use the ANC-1 form, for rebates of up to $1,500 per household.
 What each program pays
 ANCHOR pays homeowners earning $150,000 or less $1,500, and those earning $150,001 to $250,000 $1,000. Renters earning up to $150,000 get $450. Those 65 or older get $700. Senior homeowners no longer get the $250 add-on because of Stay NJ. Senior renters kept theirs.
 Stay NJ pays up to $6,500 for incomes of $100,000 or less, $5,000 up to $150,000 and $4,000 up to $200,000. Those payments are scheduled for February and May 2027. Under the budget Sherrill signed, the program's income ceiling dropped to $200,000 from $500,000.
 Its allocation fell to $756 million from more than $1 billion.
 Senior Freeze reimburses income-eligible seniors and disabled homeowners for local property tax increases. Lawmakers set aside $345 million for it. The income limit for the 2025 tax year is $172,475.
 How to apply and where to get help
 You can find the forms at the state's online application site (nj.gov). Online filing requires identity verification through ID.me, so have a driver's license, state ID, passport card or passport ready. You may need additional documents.
 Seniors should gather 2024 and 2025 income paperwork, such as NJ-1040s and Social Security statements, along with total property taxes billed for both years. Applicants under 65 need 2025 figures only. Waiting costs time.
 A filing on deadline day could mean a payment as late as about Jan. 31, 2027, according to Treasury information cited by NJ101.5.
 The Property Tax Relief Hotline is (888) 238-1233. Regional information centers operate in Cranford, Fair Lawn, Freehold, Galloway and Trenton. A calendar of filing events is on the state events page.
 Residents who want to follow related coverage can browse South Jersey real estate and South Jersey local news .
 Watch for scams. The state warns against clicking links or sharing personal information in unsolicited texts or emails about relief benefits. To check a payment, use the state's status checker with a Social Security number or ITIN and a ZIP code.
 If you have not filed, submit your application at propertytaxreliefapp.nj.gov before Nov. 2. Then follow the Division of Taxation's relief page for updates.
